newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: U.S. diplomat urges Taleban action on drugs.
newsitem.headline: U.S. diplomat urges Taleban action on drugs.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban militia has renewed a pledge to fight the drug trade, but a U.S. official said on Wednesday that promises were not enough.
"The words sound nice, but we would like to see the action," said the Islamabad-based official, who asked not to be named.
Afghanistan is one of the world's biggest opium suppliers producing about 2,300 tonnes in 1996, according to the U.N. International Drug Control Programme.
The Taleban control most of the richest poppy-growing areas and smuggling routes.

Taleban-controlled radio said that Mullah Mohammad Hassan, deputy leader of the Taleban's ruling council, had told a visiting U.S. diplomat on Tuesday that the Islamic movement deserved greater international support and recognition.
No country has formally recognised the administration set up in Kabul after the Taleban seized the Afghan capital on September 27 and imposed its purist version of Islam there.
The visit by John Holzman, deputy chief of mission at the U.S. embassy in Islamabad, was the highest-level contact between Washington and the Taleban since the capture of Kabul.

A U.S. official described the visit as part of routine contacts with Afghan factions that complemented talks Holzman held last month with opposition leaders, including General Abdul Rashid Dostum, in the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif.

"In order to respect the will of the Afghan people, the international community should further strengthen its support for the Islamic State of Afghanistan and expand its cooperation with the Afghan people and their Islamic state," the radio quoted Hassan as telling Holzman.
He said the Taleban were also committed to combating Afghanistan's thriving narcotics trade.
"The campaign against the production and trafficking in drugs is not only one of the major goals of the Islamic state but also a religious duty of ours," Hassan said.

The U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency said in a report last year that the Taleban had "reached de facto agreements with the cultivators and perhaps even traffickers to limit their attack on opium cultivation and domestic drug abuse".

Holzman's visit to Kabul precedes a planned regional tour by Robin Raphel, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for South Asian Affairs, who is due to visit Pakistan, Bangladesh, India and Sri Lanka in late January and early February.
State Department officials said on Tuesday that Raphel would not visit Afghanistan, but might meet in Pakistan members of various Afghan factions, including the Taleban movement.
